caveats: The Montauk Point Lighthouse was NOT physically relocated in 1996. That year the Montauk Historical Society took ownership. Relocation was studied by USACE and rejected in favor of a stone revetment.

USGS Hapke 2010/2011 Long Island regional net rates are dominated by nourished/engineered western barrier beaches; they are not Montauk-specific. Use the OFR 2010-1119 transect shapefiles for Montauk.
Hapke text (p. 43) writes long-term Long Island net as '−0.08 m/yr' but Table 9a lists +0.08 ± 0.2 m/yr and calls the net accretional. Table 9a is used here.

CARP 0.5–2.5 ft/yr (Downtown Montauk and Ditch Plains) is from GZA 2020 workshop slides citing 1983–2016 shoreline-change trends. USGS long-term (1800s–2007) means at those sites are smaller. Different methods and periods.
News volumes (e.g. 500,000 cy placed in 2024) can differ from FIMP design volumes (450,000 cy). Both are recorded with their sources.
Lake Montauk / Soundview is a north-shore (Block Island Sound) problem driven by jetties interrupting east-to-west littoral drift. USGS OFR 2010-1118/1119 covers the open-ocean south shore only.

studies.title: National Assessment of Shoreline Change: Historical Shoreline Change along the New England and Mid-Atlantic Coasts
studies.authors: Cheryl J. Hapke, Emily A. Himmelstoss, Meredith G. Kratzmann, Jeffrey H. List, E. Robert Thieler / U.S. Geological Survey
studies.note: The standard USGS national shoreline-change assessment. Long Island as a whole looks nearly stable or slightly accretional because western nourished barriers pull the average; Montauk itself is a bluffed erosional headland and must be read from the transect GIS, not the regional mean.

studies.title: National Assessment of Shoreline Change: A GIS Compilation of Vector Shorelines and Associated Shoreline Change Data for the New England and Mid-Atlantic Coasts
studies.authors: Emily A. Himmelstoss, Meredith G. Kratzmann, Cheryl Hapke, E. Robert Thieler, Jeffrey List / USGS
studies.note: The plottable GIS. Use LongIsland_LT.shp LRR (m/yr, negative = erosion) and LongIsland_shorelines.shp dates 1830–2007 to overlay Montauk.

studies.title: Coastal Assessment and Resiliency Plan (CARP) — Second Public Meeting / Town of East Hampton
studies.authors: GZA GeoEnvironmental of New York, with Dodson & Flinker and Coastal Ocean Analytics, for Town of East Hampton
studies.note: The town's adopted (2022) coastal plan. It treats Downtown Montauk and Ditch Plains as the two ocean-shore erosional focus areas at 0.5–2.5 ft/yr and flags Soundview/Culloden as a separate north-shore problem.

studies.title: Fire Island Inlet to Montauk Point Reformulation Study / General Reevaluation Report and Final EIS (Recommended Plan: Montauk feeder beach)
studies.authors: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, New York District
studies.note: FIMP's Montauk feature is a repeating feeder beach, not a seawall: ~450,000 cy every four years for 30 years, intended to feed the westward longshore system and bury the 2016 geobags.

studies.title: The Downtown Montauk Stabilization Project Frequently Asked Questions (as of November 18, 2015)
studies.note: Post-Sandy Downtown Montauk was so stripped that USACE built a 3,100-ft buried geotextile-bag dune (2015–16) as a one-time stabilizer until the FIMP feeder beach could be built.

studies.title: Montauk Point, NY, Hurricane and Storm Damage Reduction / Lighthouse Revetment Project (2005 Feasibility Report & EIS; 2017 Hurricane Sandy Limited Re-evaluation Report; 2021–2023 construction)
studies.authors: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, New York District, with NYS, Montauk Historical Society, NYS Parks, Town of East Hampton
studies.note: The lighthouse was never moved. USACE repeatedly chose armor-stone revetment over relocation. Distance-to-bluff shrank from ~300 ft (1796) to ~75 ft (1990s–2006) and is cited as <50–100 ft in later Corps fact sheets — then the 2021–23 revetment rebuilt the toe, including Turtle Cove.

studies.title: Inventory of Sand Borrow Sites along New York's Ocean Shoreline & their sustainable management
studies.authors: Henry Bokuniewicz and Haibo Huang / Stony Brook University for BOEM (M14AC00001)
studies.note: The best single synthesis of why Montauk bluffs matter: they start the south-shore sand conveyor, but every published budget finds they supply far less sand than is moving past Fire Island. Net transport is westward.

studies.title: Coastal Bluff Recession and Impacts on Littoral Transport: Special Reference to Montauk, NY
studies.authors: Frank S. Buonaiuto Jr. and Henry Bokuniewicz / Shore & Beach (ASBPA)
studies.note: The only peer-reviewed Montauk-specific bluff-volume paper. Recession is highly variable cove-to-headland; armoring the bluffs would cut the already-small sand feed to beaches down-drift.

studies.title: Impact of Navigation and Shore Protection Structures on Coastal Erosion and Storm Damage Reduction: Lake Montauk Harbor, Asharoken, and Goldsmith Inlet, New York
studies.authors: Applied Coastal Research and Engineering (for a DHS / coastal-structures assessment)
studies.note: The quantitative north-shore sediment budget: the 1926 jetties trap sand on the east side and starve Soundview / Culloden to the west. Applied Coastal's bypass prescription is ~6,700 cy/yr plus a ~480,000 cy restoration fill.

studies.title: Lake Montauk Harbor Navigation Improvement Project, NY
studies.authors: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, New York District, with Town of East Hampton
studies.note: Federal practice now explicitly places inlet-dredged sand on the eroded west (Soundview-side) beach — the bypass the jetties have needed since 1926. Volume of this deepening (110,000 cy) is a one-time construction fill, not the 6,700 cy/yr maintenance figure.

studies.title: Coastal Dune Restoration – Ditch Plains Beach (Town Board work session, 15 October 2024)
studies.authors: Coastal Science & Engineering (CSE) for Town of East Hampton
studies.note: The winter 2023–24 storms cut the Ditch Plains dune from ~1,925 cy to ~544 cy above MSL. The town's FEMA-oriented rebuild is on the order of 50,000–54,000 cy over ~2,700 ft — Ditch Plains is not in the FIMP feeder-beach template.

studies.title: Erosion Threatens Blufftop Trails in Montauk
studies.authors: Christopher Walsh quoting East Hampton Town Land Management (Hugh Gaites) / The East Hampton Star
studies.note: A rare local, documented bluff-top measurement next to Ditch Plains: about 0.9 ft/yr over 60 years, matching a one-year stake average of 0.88 ft/yr. Secondary news, but the numbers are attributed to town staff using dated air photos and bunkers.

studies.title: Coastal Erosion Hazard Areas (Article 34 ECL; 6 NYCRR Part 505) — maps and GIS for Long Island / East Hampton
studies.authors: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
studies.note: Any Montauk reach mapped as a Structural Hazard Area is, by legal definition, receding ≥1 ft/yr long-term. Overlay the REST services on a map; confirm against the official paper/PDF CEHA sheets.

studies.title: National Shoreline Change — GIS compilation of vector shorelines and shoreline-change data from the 1800s to the 2010s for the coast of Long Island Sound, New York and Connecticut
studies.authors: Rachel E. Henderson, Meredith Kratzmann, Amy Farris, Erika Lentz, Emily Himmelstoss / USGS Woods Hole
studies.note: Use this 2025 Sound-shore data release — not the 2010 ocean-shore product — to map Soundview Drive, Culloden, and Lake Montauk Harbor.

studies.title: Lake Montauk / Montauk Harbor jetties — construction history and downdrift effects (assembled from USACE CHL structure history, Cangemi v. United States, Town of East Hampton, Montauk Library)
studies.authors: Multiple: USACE (structure history table); E.D.N.Y. Cangemi litigation; Town of East Hampton; Montauk Library archives
studies.note: The inlet is artificial (1926). Jetties have trapped sand on the east and starved the west for a century. That is the Soundview Drive problem. The 2025–26 deepening finally places ~110,000 cy on that west beach.

usgs_site_box_rates.note: Computed 2026-08-23 from USGS OFR 2010-1119 LongIsland_LT.shp (LRR, m/yr) and LongIsland_ST.shp (EPR, m/yr). Negative = landward/erosion. Site boxes are approximate WGS84 rectangles chosen for this compilation; they are NOT official USGS analysis units. 1 m = 3.28084 ft.
